title: Bees and the Food We Eat
summary: How bees carry pollen between flowers so plants can make fruit and seeds, which foods depend on them, why bees are in danger, and how people can help.
poll: Everyone, not just farmers, should help protect bees.

versions.title: Bees Help Us Eat
versions.text:
Do you like apples? Do you like nuts? Then thank a bee!

A plant must make seeds. Most plants need help to do this. A flower makes a fine dust. It is called pollen. The pollen must move from one bloom to the next. Then the plant can make fruit and seeds.

Bees do this job. A bee lands on a bloom to drink. Its body is soft and fuzzy. Pollen sticks to its hair. When it lands on the next bloom, some pollen rubs off. This is called pollination.

Some bees shake a bloom. They buzz hard. The pollen falls out. This helps some plants.

Lots of our food needs bees. Apples and nuts need them. But not all food does. Wind moves the pollen of wheat and rice.

There are lots of kinds of bees. Most wild bees live alone. Some dig homes in the ground.

But bees are in trouble. Some bug sprays can harm them. Farms and towns take the place of wild flowers. Then bees have less to eat.

You can help. Plant flowers. Do not use bug sprays. Put out a dish of water. Small acts help bees. And bees help our crops.

versions.title: Bees and the Food We Eat
versions.text:
Do you like apples, almonds, or melons? If you do, you should thank a bee. Without bees, we would have much less of these foods.

Most flowering plants cannot make seeds on their own. A flower makes a fine dust called pollen. This pollen must travel to another flower of the same kind. This is called pollination. Once it happens, the flower can grow fruit and seeds.

Bees are great at this job. A bee visits a flower to drink nectar, a sweet liquid. Its body is covered in soft, branched hairs, so pollen sticks to it. When the bee lands on the next flower, some of the pollen rubs off.

Some bees use a special trick called buzz pollination. They hold on to a flower and shake their bodies very fast. The shaking makes the pollen fall out. Tomatoes and blueberries get pollen this way.

Scientists think that about three out of four of the world's main food crops get help from bees and other animals. Almond trees need bees almost completely. But not every crop needs them. Wind carries the pollen of wheat and rice. In Saudi Arabia, farmers pollinate date palms by hand.

There are more than 20,000 species, or kinds, of bees. Most wild bees live alone, not in hives, and many nest in the ground.

Today, bees face real dangers. Some pesticides, which are chemicals that kill pests, can harm bees. Bees also lose their habitat, the natural home where they find food, when farms and cities take the place of wildflowers.

People can help by planting flowers, using fewer pesticides, and putting out dishes of water. The United Nations even holds World Bee Day every May 20.

versions.title: Bees and the Food We Eat
versions.text:
Do you enjoy apples, almonds, or melons? If you do, you should thank a bee, because many of these foods might not exist without these hardworking insects, which quietly help to feed the world.

Most flowering plants cannot produce seeds on their own, because a flower makes a fine dust called pollen that must travel to another flower of the same species, a process called pollination. Once a flower has been pollinated, it can develop fruit and seeds, but when too little pollen arrives, many crops produce smaller or oddly shaped fruit.

Bees are especially effective pollinators. A bee visits a flower to drink nectar, a sugary liquid, and because its body is covered in soft, branched hairs, pollen clings to it. When the bee lands on the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off, and many bees also pack extra pollen into special baskets on their back legs so that they can carry it home to feed their young.

Some bees use a technique called buzz pollination, in which they grab a flower and vibrate their bodies so rapidly that the pollen shakes loose, and bumblebees pollinate tomatoes and blueberries in this way.

Scientists estimate that about three out of four of the world's main food crops benefit from pollinators such as bees. Almond trees depend on bees almost entirely, so each spring beekeepers in California move around two million hives into almond orchards. However, not every crop requires them, since wind carries the pollen of wheat and rice, and in Saudi Arabia, farmers pollinate date palms by hand.

There are more than 20,000 species of bees, and most wild bees live alone instead of in hives, often nesting in the ground.

Today, bees face serious dangers. Some pesticides, which are chemicals that kill pests, can harm bees, and tiny parasites called mites attack honeybee hives. Bees also lose their habitat, the natural home where they find food, when farms and cities replace wildflowers.

People can help by planting flowers, using fewer pesticides, and providing shallow dishes of water, and to raise awareness, the United Nations celebrates World Bee Day every year on May 20.

When the bee alights on the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off, and many bees also pack additional pollen into specialized baskets on their hind legs so that they can carry it home to nourish their young.

Some bees employ a technique called buzz pollination, in which they grip a flower and vibrate their bodies so rapidly that the pollen shakes loose, and bumblebees pollinate tomatoes and blueberries in this manner.

However, not every crop requires them, since wind carries the pollen of wheat and rice, and in Saudi Arabia, farmers pollinate date palms by hand.

versions.title: Bees and the Food We Eat
versions.text:
Do you enjoy apples, almonds, or melons? If you do, you should thank a bee, because many of these foods might not exist without these industrious insects, which quietly help to nourish the world's population.

Most flowering plants cannot produce seeds independently, because a flower manufactures a fine dust called pollen that must travel to another flower of the identical species, a process called pollination. Once a flower has been pollinated, it can develop fruit and seeds, but when insufficient pollen arrives, numerous crops produce smaller or irregularly shaped fruit.

Bees are exceptionally effective pollinators, partly because a single forager may visit dozens of blossoms during one excursion; a bee visits a flower to consume nectar, a sugary liquid, and because its body is covered in soft, branched hairs, pollen adheres to it. Whenever the bee alights on the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off, and many bees also pack additional pollen into specialized baskets on their hind legs so that they can transport it home to nourish their developing young.

Some bees employ a technique called buzz pollination, in which they grip a flower and vibrate their bodies so rapidly that the pollen shakes loose, and bumblebees pollinate tomatoes and blueberries in this manner.

Scientists estimate that approximately three out of four of the world's principal food crops benefit from pollinators such as bees, and because almond trees depend on bees almost entirely, each spring commercial beekeepers in California transport around two million hives into almond orchards. Nevertheless, not every crop requires them, since wind distributes the pollen of wheat and rice, and in Saudi Arabia, farmers pollinate date palms manually.

There are more than 20,000 species of bees, and most wild bees live solitary lives instead of inhabiting hives, frequently nesting underground.

Today, bees confront considerable dangers. Certain pesticides, which are chemicals that kill pests, can harm bees, and microscopic parasites called mites attack honeybee colonies, while bees also lose their habitat, the natural environment where they find food, when agricultural fields and expanding cities replace wildflowers.

People can help by cultivating flowers, using fewer pesticides, and providing shallow dishes of water, and to raise public awareness, the United Nations celebrates World Bee Day annually on May 20. Such modest efforts, multiplied across communities, can make a genuine difference.

wrong.C: Wheat is only one small detail.
wrong.D: The article tells how to help bees, not keep them out.

questions.why: When bees shake a flower, they make it move quickly, so the pollen falls out.

questions.stem: What happens when a bee lands on the next flower?

The flower turns into a bee.

wrong.A: Fewer bees means less fruit, not more.
wrong.B: An apple farm would not change into wheat.

wrong.D: Water does not turn into pollen.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with ways you can help?

To show that only farmers can do anything to help bees
To give readers simple steps to protect bees
To explain how wind moves pollen

wrong.A: The article does not explain how to build a hive.
wrong.B: The article says you can help too, not only farmers.
wrong.D: Wind is mentioned earlier, not in the ending.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say protecting bees is only a job for farmers and beekeepers. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that protecting bees is only a job for farmers and beekeepers. The article explains that bees face dangers like pesticides and the loss of habitat when farms and cities replace wildflowers, problems that ordinary people contribute to and can also help fix. For example, anyone can plant flowers, use fewer pesticides, and put out shallow dishes of water for bees, actions that do not require being a farmer or a beekeeper. Since scientists estimate that most of the world's food crops rely on pollinators, raising awareness and protecting bees is everyone's responsibility, not only the job of people working in orchards.
